newsitem.title: GERMANY: SOCCER-BERLINERS BID TO GIVE GERMANY A CAPITAL TEAM.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-BERLINERS BID TO GIVE GERMANY A CAPITAL TEAM.

text.p: London has five, Madrid boasts three, Rome has two. Alone among major European capitals, Berlin cannot muster a single top-flight soccer club.

Remarkably, the biggest city in the land of the European champions is not represented in the Bundesliga. Now, at long last, Berlin is trying to produce teams to match its status as capital of a reunited Germany at the heart of a new Europe.
Leading the charge to give Berlin as prominent a place in the league tables as it has in the history books is the city's best-supported side, Hertha.
The second division club has teamed up with media giant Bertelsmann in a multi-million dollar drive to hit the big time.
"The potential here is bigger than anywhere else in Germany," Hertha manager Carl-Heinz Ruehl said. "We've got four million people who don't have a single Bundesliga club."

Hertha certainly have tradition on their side. Formed in 1892, they were German champions in 1930 and 1931, founder members of the Bundesliga in 1963 and have had several spells in the top flight since then, most recently in the 1990-91 season.
Ruehl knows the reason his side and others in the city now struggle to get attendance figures above a few thousand is not because Berliners have no appetite for the game.
Hansa Rostock, eastern Germany's only representative in the Bundesliga, drew 60,000 people to the Olympic stadium when they played one of their "home" games in Berlin last season.
Some of Germany's best players -- like Euro 96 stars Christian Ziege and Thomas Haessler and World Cup veteran Pierre Littbarski -- have come from Berlin.
But while Berliners may love the game, their strong sense of pride means they are not prepared to tolerate sloppy standards. Hertha finished 14th in the second division last season.

"Berliners don't accept mediocrity," commented Martin Bader, a marketing manager with Bertelsmann's sports-minded television subsidiary Ufa, who has come in to oversee the day-to-day running of the new business.
The city's ice hockey and basketball teams draw big crowds simply because they are successful, even though they have no tradition comparable with the soccer clubs.

Bertelsmann has invested heavily in Hertha, attracting experienced professionals such as Axel Kruse from VfB Stuttgart. The team are now challenging for a promotion place and aim to be in the Bundesliga within the next two seasons.
But the sleeping giants, who appropriately sell nightcaps in the club colours of blue and white in their souvenir shop, are not the only West Berliners with big ideas.
Tennis Borussia Berlin are languishing in the level below the second division -- the regional league -- but they aim to be in the Bundesliga by the end of the century.

Located in the plush suburb of Charlottenburg, they may not have the working class mass appeal of Hertha but they do have one thing in common with their rivals -- they have also joined forces with big business to fund their drive to the top.
An insurance firm, Goettinger Gruppe, is providing financial backing and marketing expertise for the side.

Helmut van der Lahr, spokesman for the marketing firm set up by Goettinger to make the most of the club's potential, believes Berlin has lagged far behind other cities in terms of modern sports management because of its Cold War past.

"There was no normality here as it developed in the rest of West Germany," he said, pointing out that businessmen in the city got used to surviving on subsidies Bonn pumped into West Berlin to make it a showcase of capitalism.
"The island situation continued for a long time and has left its imprint on a lot of realities. The structure of most of the clubs in the city is simply old fashioned."
On the other side of the city, the history of the clubs is intertwined with the whims of its former communist masters.
"We have to plant smaller acorns for the time being," acknowledged Friedrich-Otto Schoenig, manager of Union Berlin.
The proud little club bounced between the first and second divisions of the old East Germany, despite various handicaps.
Often the club's top players would be forced to transfer to local rivals Dynamo, the club of the feared Stasi secret police.
Dynamo could pluck players from clubs across East Germany without fear of protest. While they enjoyed the privileges of party endorsement, Union were often left out in the cold.

After the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989, Union embraced capitalism in a bid to make the big time. Seven years on, Union are burdened with that legacy, too, having to sell players to pay their considerable debts and survive in the regional league.

Union fans could be forgiven for taking some comfort from how their mighty local rivals have fallen. Stigmatised by their past, Dynamo have transformed themselves into FC Berlin and now play alongside Union and Tennis Borussia in the regional league.
Hefty transfer income from selling off top players like Andreas Thom seems to have been of little help.
So while Union and FC Berlin concentrate on balancing the books and Tennis Borussia first have to get out of the regional league, Berlin's hopes for the Bundesliga rest with Hertha.

One of the club's toughest tests may not be on the field but in welding together the world of big business and the traditions of an old soccer club. Already there have been clashes between the businessmen and the sports specialists.
But the side are performing creditably, establishing themselves in the top half of the table, and the bosses are keen to show they are working as a team, too.
"We even go to away games" enthused marketing man Bader. "We don't have to go but we do, because it's great fun."
